title: Roman teachers charge Calvin and the Reformed with taking free choice away from man
source_text: I. Plerique Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Calvino, & aliis qui cum eo in Religionis negotio sentiunt, tribuere solent quod ab homine tollant liberum arbitrium, eumque omni libertate in agendo spolient, aut saltem doceant in eo liberum Arbitrium per peccatum penitus amissum & extinctum fuisse. Istud videre est apud Bailium Jesuitam in Catechesi quam refutat Rivetus in summa Controversiarum Tract. 4. quaest. 4. Ubi disputat contra Reformatos, quasi liberum hominis arbitrium simpliciter negarent: & apud Martinum Becanum Jesuitam alterum qui dicit Lutheranos & Calvinistas affirmare per peccatum primi parentis penitus sublatum esse liberum arbitrium. In summa Theol. Scholast. Tract. 1. cap. 2. quaest. 9.
pass_a_gloss: Most Doctors of the Roman Church are wont to attribute to Calvin, and to others who agree with him in the business of Religion, that they take away free choice from man, and strip him of all liberty in acting, or at least teach that in him free Choice was wholly lost and extinguished through sin. This may be seen in Bailius the Jesuit in the Catechism which Rivet refutes in the summary of Controversies Tract. 4. quest. 4. Where he disputes against the Reformed, as though they simply denied the free choice of man: and in Martin Becanus another Jesuit who says that Lutherans and Calvinists affirm that through the sin of the first parent free choice was wholly taken away. In the summa of Scholastic Theology Tract. 1. chap. 2. quest. 9.
pass_b_english: Most teachers of the Roman Church commonly accuse Calvin and those who share his religious position of removing free choice from man and stripping him of any freedom in what he does. At the least, they say, these men teach that sin destroyed free choice in man altogether.

One example is the Jesuit Bailly, in the catechism that Rivet answers in his Summary of Controversies (treatise 4, question 4). There Bailly argues against the Reformed as if they flatly denied that man has free choice.

Another is the Jesuit Martin Becanus. In his Summa of Scholastic Theology (treatise 1, chapter 2, question 9) he says that Lutherans and Calvinists hold that the sin of our first parent completely did away with free choice.

choices.why: Le Blanc's whole locus turns on the faculty, not on a state of liberty; 'free choice' keeps the scholastic term without the later connotations of 'free will' as a separate power.
